title: Length of Last Word
directAnswer: Scan from the END of the string. First skip any trailing spaces, then count consecutive non-space characters until you hit a space or the start. That count is the answer — O(n) time, O(1) space, no split() needed.

remember.pattern: Reverse scan with two phases (skip trailing, then count)
remember.formula:
i = len(s) - 1
while i >= 0 and s[i] == ' ': i -= 1   # skip trailing spaces
length = 0
while i >= 0 and s[i] != ' ': i -= 1; length += 1
return length
rules: **Strip trailing spaces first.** Inputs like `"Hello World   "` end in spaces; counting before skipping them gives 0.
**Walk from the right, not the left.** You only need the *last* word, so scanning from the end avoids tracking every word.
**Stop at the first space after the word** — that boundary marks the start of the last word.
**No leading-space worry once you scan right-to-left**; the right-to-left walk naturally ignores everything before the last word.
**`split()` works but is wasteful** — it allocates the whole word list when you only need one length.
whenToUse: You need information about only the last (or first) token, not all tokens
Input may have arbitrary trailing/leading whitespace to normalize
Constant extra space is desired — avoid building intermediate arrays
A single linear pass from one end suffices
antiSignals: You need every word's length / all tokens → split() is justified
Words are separated by arbitrary delimiters, not just spaces → use a proper tokenizer/regex
You must modify words in place → different problem (Reverse Words)
The 'word' definition includes punctuation rules → needs explicit char classification
remember.takeaway: When a problem only cares about the boundary element (last word, last digit, last segment), scanning from the relevant end with O(1) space beats splitting the whole input. Two tiny phases — skip the trailing noise, then count the real thing — solve it cleanly.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you handle trailing whitespace correctly and whether you reach for an O(1)-space reverse scan instead of reflexively calling split() and indexing the last element.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Counting from the right without first skipping trailing spaces, so "a " returns 0; or using s.split(' ')[-1] which breaks on multiple spaces by yielding empty strings.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Mention that split() is fine but allocates the whole list; offer the O(1)-space two-phase reverse scan and note the trailing-space trap explicitly before coding.

problemStatement:
Given a string `s` consisting of words and spaces, return the **length of the last word** in the string.

A **word** is a maximal substring consisting of non-space characters only.
constraints: s consists of only English letters and spaces ' '
There is at least one word in s
understanding: Find the rightmost run of non-space characters and report its length. Spaces can appear anywhere — including trailing — so the core difficulty is correctly locating where the last word ends and begins.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the string have trailing spaces?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — e.g. "Hello World   ". This is the main trap: you must skip trailing spaces before counting.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can there be multiple spaces between words?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. That's why naive s.split(' ')[-1] is risky — it can produce empty strings. split() with no argument (Python) collapses runs, which is safer.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the string guaranteed to contain at least one word?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, per constraints, so we never return on an all-spaces string. Still good to know the guarantee.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are there any non-letter, non-space characters?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — only English letters and the space character. So a 'word' is simply a run of letters.

examples.explanation: The last word is "World", which has length 5.

examples.input: s = "   fly me   to   the moon  "
examples.explanation: After skipping trailing spaces, the last word is "moon" (length 4).

approaches.name: Split and Take Last (Library)
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first as the obvious one-liner, then critique its allocation and the multiple-spaces footgun.
hints: The language can tokenize the string for you. What does split do, and which element do you then want?
In Python, str.split() with no argument collapses runs of whitespace and ignores leading/trailing spaces — convenient here.
Split into words, then take the last word and return its length. Beware split(' ') with an explicit space argument: it keeps empty strings between consecutive spaces.
approaches.complexityReasoning: split() walks the whole string once (O(n)) and allocates a list of all words (O(n) extra space). Indexing the last element and taking its length is O(1).
approaches.explanation:
The most direct solution leans on the standard library: split the string into a list of words and return the length of the last one. It reads almost like the problem statement, which is its main virtue in an interview — you can produce it in seconds and then immediately discuss its weaknesses.

**Why the splitting variant matters.** In Python, `s.split()` *with no argument* is the safe form: it treats any run of whitespace as a single delimiter and discards leading and trailing whitespace, so `"  a  b  ".split()` is `['a', 'b']`. Contrast `s.split(' ')` *with an explicit space*: that splits on every single space and keeps the empty strings between consecutive spaces, so `"a  b".split(' ')` is `['a', '', 'b']` — taking `[-1]` could hand you an empty string from a trailing space. In Java, `s.trim().split("\\s+")` is the parallel safe form. **Knowing which split semantics you're using is the difference between correct and subtly broken.**

**Why we don't always ship it.** Splitting allocates a list holding *every* word even though we only ever need the last one's length. For a string with thousands of words that's a lot of throwaway memory. The interviewer who asks 'can you do it in O(1) extra space?' is steering you toward the reverse scan. So present this as the readable baseline, then offer the optimal.

**Why it's still worth stating.** It's the version you'd actually write in production where clarity beats micro-optimization, and it demonstrates you know your language's string API. Just be explicit about the whitespace-collapsing semantics so the interviewer trusts you understand the edge cases.
approaches.insight: The whole correctness of the one-liner hinges on whether your language's split collapses whitespace runs. `split()` (no arg, Python) and `trim().split("\\s+")` (Java) are safe; `split(' ')` is a trap. Naming that distinction unprompted signals real fluency.

approaches.name: Reverse Scan, O(1) Space (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer for the O(1)-space follow-up. Frame it as two phases: skip trailing spaces, then count the word.
hints: You only need the LAST word. Which end of the string should you start from to avoid tracking every word?
Start at the last index. First move left past any trailing spaces. Where you stop is the last character of the last word.
Now count leftward while characters are non-space. Stop at the first space (or the string start). The count is the length.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single index walks from the end leftward at most n positions across both phases combined. Only a couple of integer variables are used, so O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Because the question asks only about the *last* word, the efficient move is to scan from the **right end** of the string and stop the moment we've measured one word. This avoids allocating any list and uses only a pointer and a counter.

**Phase one — skip trailing spaces.** Inputs like `"Hello World   "` end in spaces, and the last word's final character sits to the *left* of them. So we start `i` at the last index and decrement while `s[i]` is a space. When this loop stops, `i` points at the last non-space character — the true end of the last word. **Skipping this phase is the single most common bug**: counting immediately from `len(s) - 1` on a space-terminated string yields 0 because the first thing you see is a space.

**Phase two — count the word.** From the end of the last word, we keep walking left and incrementing a counter while `s[i]` is a non-space character. The loop also guards `i >= 0` so a string that is a single word (no leading space) terminates at the start instead of indexing out of bounds. When we hit a space — the gap before the last word — or run off the front, the counter holds exactly the last word's length.

**Why right-to-left beats left-to-right here.** A left-to-right scan would have to track the length of *every* word, resetting on each space, because it can't know which word is last until it reaches the end. Scanning from the right, the *first* word we encounter is the one we want, so we can return as soon as we've measured it. Same O(n) worst case, but conceptually simpler and with no wasted bookkeeping. This is the general lesson: when only a boundary element matters, start from that boundary.
approaches.insight: Two tight phases — 'skip the trailing noise' then 'measure the real thing' — is a reusable shape. You'll see the same skeleton in trimming, in parsing the last token of a path, and in reading a number off the end of a string.

pitfalls: Skipping phase 1 — counting from the last index directly returns 0 on a trailing-space input.
Omitting the i >= 0 guard in phase 2 — a single-word string indexes out of bounds.
Using a for loop that doesn't break, recomputing across every word unnecessarily.

commonMistakes: Counting from the end without first skipping trailing spaces — returns 0 on "word ".
Using split(' ')[-1] with an explicit space, which yields empty strings on multiple/trailing spaces.
Forgetting the bounds guard in the count loop, causing an out-of-bounds on a single-word input.
Scanning left-to-right and tracking every word when only the last one matters.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Not skipping trailing spaces
commonMistakesDetailed.why: On "Hello World   " the last index is a space, so counting immediately gives 0. You must move past trailing spaces first.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
i = len(s) - 1
length = 0
while i >= 0 and s[i] != ' ':
    length += 1
    i -= 1
return length  # returns 0 on trailing spaces
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
i = len(s) - 1
while i >= 0 and s[i] == ' ':
    i -= 1
length = 0
while i >= 0 and s[i] != ' ':
    length += 1
    i -= 1
return length

commonMistakesDetailed.title: split(' ') with explicit space
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Explicit-space split keeps empty strings between consecutive spaces, so [-1] can be '' on trailing/multiple spaces.
commonMistakesDetailed.good: return len(s.split()[-1])  # no-arg split collapses whitespace

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing bounds guard in count loop
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Without i >= 0, a single-word string like 'a' decrements i to -1 and then indexes s[-1] (Java throws, Python wraps to the wrong char).
